The **[Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades](Izz_ad-Din_al-Qassam_Brigades "Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades")** is Hamas's military wing. By the time of the Al-Aqsa Intifada, Hamas's laboratories had devised a primitive form of rocketry, the Qassam 1, which they first launched in October 2000, carrying a 500 g (18 oz) warhead with a throw range of 4 km (2.5 mi). Both propellant and the explosive were manufactured from chemical fertilizers, though TNT was also tried.[[105]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTESabry201565-118) Over the next five years of the conflict, a 3 kg (6.6 lb)-warhead-armed version with a strike range of 6 km (3.7 mi)–8 km (5.0 mi), the Qassam 2, was also produced[[106]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTENajibFriedrich2007107-119) and in an incremental rise, these rocket types were fired towards Israeli settlements along the Gaza Strip: 4 in 2001, 35 in 2002, 155 in 2003, 281 in 2004, and 179 in 2005. By 2005, the Qassam 3 had been engineered with a 12 km (7.5 mi)–14 km (8.7 mi) range and a 15 kl (530 cu ft) warhead. In the 2014 war its advanced rocketry reached Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and <Haifa>.[[59]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJefferis2016119-71)

While the number of members is known only to the Brigades leadership, Israel estimates the Brigades have a core of several hundred members who receive [military style training](Military_training "Military training"), including training in Iran and in <Syria> (before the Syrian Civil War).[[109]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGuidère2012173-122) Additionally, the brigades have an estimated 10,000–17,000 operatives,[[94]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShitrit201571-106)[[110]](Hamas#cite_note-FOOTNOTENajibFriedrich2007106-123) forming a backup force whenever circumstances call for reinforcements for the Brigade. Not to be confused with [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita").

See also: [List of countries by average wage](List_of_countries_by_average_wage "List of countries by average wage")

A country's [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) at [purchasing power parity](Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") (PPP) per capita is the PPP value of all final [goods and services](Goods_and_services "Goods and services") produced within an [economy](Economy "Economy") in a given year, divided by the average (or mid-year) population for the same year. This is similar to nominal GDP per capita, but adjusted for the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in each country.

In 2019, the estimated average GDP per capita (PPP) of all of the countries of the world was [Int$](International_dollar "International dollar") 18,381.[[lower-alpha 1]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-3) For rankings regarding wealth, see [list of countries by wealth per adult](List_of_countries_by_wealth_per_adult "List of countries by wealth per adult").

## Method

The [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) [per capita](Per_capita "Per capita") figures on this page are derived from PPP calculations. Such calculations are prepared by various organizations, including the <IMF> and the [World Bank](World_Bank "World Bank"). As estimates and assumptions have to be made, the results produced by different organizations for the same country are not hard facts and tend to differ, sometimes substantially, so they should be used with caution.

Comparisons of national wealth are frequently made on the basis of *nominal* GDP and [savings](Savings "Savings") (not just income), which do not reflect differences in the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in different countries (*see [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita")*); hence, using a PPP basis is arguably more useful when comparing [generalized](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/generalized "wikt:generalized") differences in [living standards](Living_standards "Living standards") between economies because PPP takes into account the relative cost of living and the [inflation rates](Inflation_rates "Inflation rates") of the countries, rather than using only [exchange rates](Exchange_rates "Exchange rates"), which may distort the real differences in income.

This is why GDP (PPP) per capita is often considered one of the indicators of a country's standard of living,[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-4)[[

You are a helpful assistant. Current date: 11-20-2023.

# Multi-Agent Delegation

When the user asks a complex question, do not attempt to answer it yourself. Break it up into smaller pieces, then use the `fork` tool to delegate each piece to a subagent. You MUST use the `join` tool to retrieve the subagent's result for each subagent you create with `fork`. Each subagent has access to the exact same tools that you do.

If you are confident you can answer the user's query without help, do not use the delegation tools.

## Writing Instructions

The instructions you give to each subagent SHOULD be a smaller piece of the instructions you were given. Do not delegate your full task to a subagent. Subagents do not have access to the information you have retrieved in prior turns or your thoughts. You must provide each subagent with the necessary context it needs in its instructions.

Your instructions to a subagent can be long, up to about 5000 characters. Each subagent is as capable as you are, but starts with a blank slate, so you must provide it specific and detailed information in its instructions.

Examples of poor instructions:
- Analyze the retrieved page to find the number of stations.
- Implement the `dfs()` function.
- Use the article to list the subway connections.
- Prove Lemma 3.
- Continue searching for the magic number.

Examples of good instructions:
- Search for the Wikipedia article for the Yamanote Line and find the number of stations on the line.
- Write a DFS function in Python with the signature `def dfs(root: Node, predicate: Callable[[Node], bool]) -> Node`. The `Node` type is a `dict` with shape `{"data": Any, "children": list[Node]}`.
- Retrieve the Wikipedia article for Shinjuku Station (pageid=123456) and list all of the subway connections.

- Search for the magic number in the given context in the index slice 10000:20000. If no magic number is present, return `null`.

---
canonical: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita
meta-viewport: width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0
title: List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita
---


Not to be confused with [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita").

See also: [List of countries by average wage](List_of_countries_by_average_wage "List of countries by average wage")

A country's [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) at [purchasing power parity](Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") (PPP) per capita is the PPP value of all final [goods and services](Goods_and_services "Goods and services") produced within an [economy](Economy "Economy") in a given year, divided by the average (or mid-year) population for the same year. This is similar to nominal GDP per capita, but adjusted for the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in each country.

In 2019, the estimated average GDP per capita (PPP) of all of the countries of the world was [Int$](International_dollar "International dollar") 18,381.[[lower-alpha 1]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-3) For rankings regarding wealth, see [list of countries by wealth per adult](List_of_countries_by_wealth_per_adult "List of countries by wealth per adult").

## Method

The [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) [per capita](Per_capita "Per capita") figures on this page are derived from PPP calculations. Such calculations are prepared by various organizations, including the <IMF> and the [World Bank](World_Bank "World Bank"). As estimates and assumptions have to be made, the results produced by different organizations for the same country are not hard facts and tend to differ, sometimes substantially, so they should be used with caution.

Comparisons of national wealth are frequently made on the basis of *nominal* GDP and [savings](Savings "Savings") (not just income), which do not reflect differences in the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in different countries (*see [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita")*); hence, using a PPP basis is arguably more useful when comparing [generalized](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/generalized "wikt:generalized") differences in [living standards](Living_standards "Living standards") between economies because PPP takes into account the relative cost of living and the [inflation rates](Inflation_rates "Inflation rates") of the countries, rather than using only [exchange rates](Exchange_rates "Exchange rates"), which may distort the real differences in income.

This is why GDP (PPP) per capita is often considered one of the indicators of a country's standard of living,[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-4)[[4]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-5) although this can be problematic because GDP per capita is not a measure of [personal income](Personal_income "Personal income"). (*See [Standard of living and GDP](Gross_domestic_product#Standard_of_living_and_GDP:_wealth_distribution_and_externalities "Gross domestic product")*.)

GDP (PPP) and GDP (PPP) per capita are usually measured by [international dollar](International_dollar "International dollar"), which is a hypothetical [currency](Currency "Currency") that has the same purchasing power in every economy as the [U.S. dollar](U.S._dollar "U.S. dollar") in the [United States](United_States "United States").

## Table

All figures are in current [international dollars](International_dollar "International dollar"), and [rounded](Rounding "Rounding") to the nearest [whole number](Integer "Integer").

*The table initially ranks each country or territory with their latest available year's estimates, and can be reranked by either of the sources.*

* *Nearly all country links in the table connect to articles titled "Income in (*country *or* territory*)" or to "Economy of (*country *or* territory*)".*

Not to be confused with [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita").

See also: [List of countries by average wage](List_of_countries_by_average_wage "List of countries by average wage")

A country's [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) at [purchasing power parity](Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") (PPP) per capita is the PPP value of all final [goods and services](Goods_and_services "Goods and services") produced within an [economy](Economy "Economy") in a given year, divided by the average (or mid-year) population for the same year. This is similar to nominal GDP per capita, but adjusted for the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in each country.

In 2019, the estimated average GDP per capita (PPP) of all of the countries of the world was [Int$](International_dollar "International dollar") 18,381.[[lower-alpha 1]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-3) For rankings regarding wealth, see [list of countries by wealth per adult](List_of_countries_by_wealth_per_adult "List of countries by wealth per adult").

## Method

The [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) [per capita](Per_capita "Per capita") figures on this page are derived from PPP calculations. Such calculations are prepared by various organizations, including the <IMF> and the [World Bank](World_Bank "World Bank"). As estimates and assumptions have to be made, the results produced by different organizations for the same country are not hard facts and tend to differ, sometimes substantially, so they should be used with caution.

Comparisons of national wealth are frequently made on the basis of *nominal* GDP and [savings](Savings "Savings") (not just income), which do not reflect differences in the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in different countries (*see [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita")*); hence, using a PPP basis is arguably more useful when comparing [generalized](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/generalized "wikt:generalized") differences in [living standards](Living_standards "Living standards") between economies because PPP takes into account the relative cost of living and the [inflation rates](Inflation_rates "Inflation rates") of the countries, rather than using only [exchange rates](Exchange_rates "Exchange rates"), which may distort the real differences in income.

This is why GDP (PPP) per capita is often considered one of the indicators of a country's standard of living,[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-4)[[4]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-5) although this can be problematic because GDP per capita is not a measure of [personal income](Personal_income "Personal income"). (*See [Standard of living and GDP](Gross_domestic_product#Standard_of_living_and_GDP:_wealth_distribution_and_externalities "Gross domestic product")*.)

GDP (PPP) and GDP (PPP) per capita are usually measured by [international dollar](International_dollar "International dollar"), which is a hypothetical [currency](Currency "Currency") that has the same purchasing power in every economy as the [U.S. dollar](U.S._dollar "U.S. dollar") in the [United States](United_States "United States").

All figures are in current [international dollars](International_dollar "International dollar"), and [rounded](Rounding "Rounding") to the nearest [whole number](Integer "Integer").

GDP (PPP) means [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") based on [purchasing power parity](Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity").
This article includes a list of countries by their forecast estimated GDP (PPP).[[2]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)#cite_note-2) Countries are sorted by GDP (PPP) forecast estimates from financial and statistical institutions that calculate using market or government official [exchange rates](Exchange_rate "Exchange rate"). The data given on this page are based on the [international dollar](Geary%E2%80%93Khamis_dollar "Geary–Khamis dollar"), a standardized unit used by economists. Certain regions that are not widely considered countries such as [Hong Kong](Hong_Kong "Hong Kong") also show up in the list if they are distinct jurisdiction areas or economic entities.

GDP comparisons using PPP are arguably more useful than those using [nominal GDP](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)") when assessing the domestic market of a state because PPP takes into account the relative cost of local goods, services and inflation rates of the country, rather than using international market exchange rates, which may distort the real differences in per capita income.[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)#cite_note-ICP-3) It is however limited when measuring financial flows between countries and when comparing the quality of same goods among countries.[[4]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)#cite_note-CallenIMF-4) PPP is often used to gauge global [poverty thresholds](Poverty_threshold "Poverty threshold") and is used by the [United Nations](United_Nations "United Nations") in constructing the [human development index](Human_development_index "Human development index").[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)#cite_note-ICP-3) These surveys such as the International Comparison Program include both tradable and non-tradable goods in an attempt to estimate a representative basket of all goods.[[3]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)#cite_note-ICP-3)

Not to be confused with [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita").

See also: [List of countries by average wage](List_of_countries_by_average_wage "List of countries by average wage")

A country's [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) at [purchasing power parity](Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity") (PPP) per capita is the PPP value of all final [goods and services](Goods_and_services "Goods and services") produced within an [economy](Economy "Economy") in a given year, divided by the average (or mid-year) population for the same year. This is similar to nominal GDP per capita, but adjusted for the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in each country.

In 2019, the estimated average GDP per capita (PPP) of all of the countries of the world was [Int$](International_dollar "International dollar") 18,381.[[lower-alpha 1]](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita#cite_note-3) For rankings regarding wealth, see [list of countries by wealth per adult](List_of_countries_by_wealth_per_adult "List of countries by wealth per adult").

## Method

The [gross domestic product](Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") (GDP) [per capita](Per_capita "Per capita") figures on this page are derived from PPP calculations. Such calculations are prepared by various organizations, including the <IMF> and the [World Bank](World_Bank "World Bank"). As estimates and assumptions have to be made, the results produced by different organizations for the same country are not hard facts and tend to differ, sometimes substantially, so they should be used with caution.

Comparisons of national wealth are frequently made on the basis of *nominal* GDP and [savings](Savings "Savings") (not just income), which do not reflect differences in the [cost of living](Cost_of_living "Cost of living") in different countries (*see [List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita](List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (nominal) per capita")*); hence, using a PPP basis is arguably more useful when comparing [generalized](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/generalized "wikt:generalized") differences in [living standards](Living_standards "Living standards") between economies because PPP takes into account the relative cost of living and the [inflation rates](Inflation_rates "Inflation rates") of the countries, rather than using only [exchange rates](Exchange_rates "Exchange rates"), which may distort the real differences in income.

Based on my research of Wikipedia articles about the economy of Australia, I found the 2023 estimated PPP (Purchasing Power Parity) per capita GDP of Australia.

## Answer

**Australia's 2023 estimated GDP (PPP) per capita is $65,366** (international dollars).

## Sources

I found this information in the Wikipedia article "List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita," which contains data from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) World Economic Outlook. The specific entry for Australia shows:

| Country | Region | 2023 Estimate | 2022 Estimate | 2021 Estimate |
|---------|--------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| Australia | Oceania | **$65,366** | $62,625 | $49,800 |

This represents Australia's GDP at purchasing power parity divided by its population, adjusted for differences in the cost of living. Australia ranks among the top countries globally for GDP (PPP) per capita.

I also found in the "Economy of Australia" article that the total GDP (PPP) for Australia in 2023 was $1.718 trillion, ranking 19th in the world by GDP (PPP).
